title: Fabrication, application, and phase formation rules in high-entropy alloys
abstract: Abstract High entropy alloys (HEAs) have become the focus of research and industrial attention as a new class of advanced engineering materials due to their exceptional properties and performance. Generally, HEAs exhibit superior performance compared to traditional alloys, especially when they form FCC or BCC single-phase solid solutions. However, achieving such systems is beyond simple mixing of elements and is not always straightforward. It strongly depends on element selection, deliberate design of compositions, processing strategies, and thermodynamic control. Given the vast compositional space of HEAs, the use of predictive tools is Inevitable. Phase formation rules, as an empirical approach, have become effective and valuable tools for accelerating the screening of single-phase FCC or BCC alloys and minimizing trial-and-error efforts due to their low cost, time-saving nature, and simplicity. In this regard, the present review elaborated quantitatively and conceptually the thermodynamic parameters such as Gibbs free energy of mixing (ΔG mix ), configurational entropy (ΔS mix ), enthalpy of mixing (ΔH mix ), and the prediction parameter for solid solution formation (Ω), along with Hume-Rothery criteria, including atomic size difference (δ), valence electron concentration (VEC), and electronegativity difference (Δχ). In addition, the processing and manufacturing routes, economic aspects, and applications of HEAs are discussed. This review provides a comprehensive overview of HEA with a practical framework from element selection, design, and fabrication techniques to the relationship between phase, properties, and performance. The present work bridges the gap between HEAs design, manufacturing processes, practical implementation, and application. Additionally, an overview of cost and manufacturing considerations has highlighted future research directions in targeted design, scalable production, and the industrial application of HEAs.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: From the Stone Age through to the present era of advanced technologies, the development of new materials has always played a fundamental role in advancing human civilization. Rapid advances in industry and technology have led to a demand for materials with specific properties and applications that can maintain excellent performance in extreme environmental conditions and exceed the capabilities of conventional alloys. In most cases, metals are not used in their pure form. The common strategy for developing traditional alloys involves selecting a primary component (base metal) based on the desired properties and adding alloying elements to create improved properties. This strategy has led to the extension of many conventional alloys, centered around one or two principal components, resulting in the development of several well-known alloy families, including ferrous alloys (e.g., steel and cast iron), aluminum alloys, and nickel-based superalloys. A class of materials inspired by these traditional systems, introduced nearly two decades ago, is high entropy alloys (HEAs).

In 2004, Cantor et al. [ 1 ] and Yeh et al. [ 2 ] independently introduced HEAs as an innovative class of metallic materials characterized by the near-equiatomic incorporation of five or more principal elements, typically ranging in concentration from 5 to 35%, in contrast to conventional alloys, which are generally composed of one or two dominant components. Later developments in HEAs removed the requirement for equimolarity and extended the definition of HEAs to include non-equimolar compositions. This significantly expanded the number of possible HEAs configurations [ 3 ]. In addition, to modify properties of the alloy, HEAs can contain elements with concentrations of less than 5%, which in turn leads to the extra expansion of the HEAs configuration systems [ 4 ]. In the literature, HEAs are also referred to as multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), or alloys with several main elements [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 ,  8 – 9 ]. This concept also encompasses non-metallic materials and has expanded its scope to high entropy materials (HEMs) [ 10 ]. Although considerably valuable studies have investigated the basic concepts, design principles, properties, and characteristics of HEAs, limited attention has been given to the manufacturing and processing aspects that greatly influence their final behavior and performance. The existing literature often overlooks the realistic interactions among alloy design, processing methods, costs, and practical applications of HEAs, which are essential for their development and industrialization. In this review, besides establishing a framework for the design of HEAs based on phase formation rules and relevant conceptual discussions, particular focus is placed on how various processing techniques (solid, liquid, and gas states) impact phase formation and performance. Additionally, aspects related to manufacturing costs, production tips, and scalability are also included, providing a more practical perspective. Overall, this work adopts a comprehensive approach, presenting design concepts, element selection, phase formation rules, processing strategies, economic considerations, and performance requirements for real-world engineering applications, thereby supporting academic and industrial research in the field of HEAs.

The structure of this review includes the following sections:

“Introduction” section  introduces the four core effects, along with the key properties of HEAs.  “Phases and mechanical performance in HEAs” section  explores the phases in HEAs and their corresponding mechanical properties.  “Applications of HEAs” section  focuses on the practical applications of HEAs across various engineering fields.  “Processing routes of HEAs: effects on microstructure, phase evolution, and properties”Section  discusses processing routes and fabrication techniques of HEAs along with their impact on microstructure, phase evolution, and overall alloy behavior.  “Techno-economic assessment of HEAs raw materials and processing routes” section  evaluates the techno-economic aspects of raw materials and processing methods.  “High entropy alloys design” section  presents HEAs design strategies with a focus on the empirical design approach.  “Challenges”Section  highlights current research challenges in the development of HEAs.  “Future perspectives” section  outlines future directions and potential areas for exploration, and  “Conclusion” section  concludes the review.

sections.heading: Four Core effects and key properties of HEAs
paragraphs: HEAs exhibit exceptional properties due to their multi-element composition, which has made them focus of interest in engineering and industry. Properties such as remarkable mechanical properties [ 38 ,  39 ] including excellent ductility [ 40 ,  41 ], wear resistance [ 42 ,  43 ], high strength and hardness [ 44 ,  45 – 46 ], good thermal stability, and reliable performance in high-temperature applications [ 47 ,  48 ], superior corrosion [ 49 ,  50 ] and oxidation resistance [ 51 ], engineerable magnetic and electrical properties [ 52 ,  53 ] make them attractive candidates for next-generation structural and functional materials. Such unique features are attributed to four effects named the core effects, including: (1) high entropy effect, (2) severe lattice distortion, (3) sluggish diffusion, and (4) cocktail effect. A deep understanding of how these effects work is fundamental to a principled and precise design of HEAs. The phase transformations, microstructure, stability, properties, performance, and overall behavior of the HEAs are affected by the Core effects. The four core effects are depicted schematically in Fig.  3 . Figure 3 The four core effects of high entropy alloys.

sections.heading: High entropy effect
paragraphs: The disorder and random distribution of atoms constituting HEAs are illustrated in Fig.  3 . The fact that HEAs, despite their elemental and chemical complexity, tend to form solid solutions with simple structures such as FCC or BCC is due to the high entropy of their system. Due to the increase in the entropy of the system, the Gibbs free energy (See Eq.  1 ) decreases, which promotes the formation and stabilization of the solid solution and reduces the tendency to separate and form complex structures. This solution is so strong in HEAs systems that the solvent and solute atoms are indistinguishable [ 2 ,  54 ,  55 ,  56 – 57 ].

sections.heading: Severe lattice distortion
paragraphs: As shown in Fig.  3 , the difference in atomic radius among the constituent elements of HEAs, which occupy random positions in the atomic lattice, causes severe distortions in the lattice structure. These distortions are reportedly more severe than those in conventional alloys. In turn, such complexity and randomness in atomic structure further increase the system’s entropy. This effect explains many of the mechanical, thermal, and electrical behaviors associated with HEAs. Additionally, disordered atomic structure results in a decrease in the intensity of XRD peaks. Since most mechanical behavior depends on the ease or difficulty of dislocation movement, severe lattice distortion makes it harder for dislocations to move, a phenomenon known as pinning, which increases strength and controls plasticity. Due to the strong scattering of electrons and their paths in the lattice, HEAs typically have high electrical resistance. This same atomic lattice disorder also impacts their thermal conductivity, reducing it and diminishing its temperature dependence [ 5 ,  54 ,  57 ,  58 ,  59 ,  60 – 61 ].

sections.heading: Sluggish diffusion
paragraphs: Sluggish diffusion refers to the reduction in the rate of atomic diffusion in the alloy structure. As shown in Fig.  3 , atoms enter the lattice in HEAs along more irregular paths compared to pure metals. It is thought that due to the high structural disorder and chemical complexity in HEAs, atoms require more energy to move, which slows down the diffusion processes. This property can increase stability at high temperatures and resistance to creep deformation, and increase activation energy [ 2 ,  3 ,  62 ,  63 ]. Tsai et al. [ 64 ] measured the diffusion coefficient of CoCrFeMnNi alloys and compared it with the diffusion coefficients of their pure metallic elements. They reported that the diffusion coefficient of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA is lower than that of the reference pure elements. Furthermore, its activation energy was also higher than that of the constituent elements. The increased fluctuation of lattice potential energy results in stronger atomic traps and blocks, which in turn raise the activation energies. This explains the sluggish diffusion observed in HEAs. It should be noted that this hypothesis (Sluggish Diffusion) has always been accompanied by doubt and has not been directly proven. This is only supported by empirical evidence and secondary observations. A few studies have been conducted in this field, and it is still not completely clear [ 62 ].

sections.heading: Cocktail effect
paragraphs:
At first glance, the term “cocktail” may evoke images of colorful and diverse drinks. Just as these drinks can produce different tastes and colors by adjusting the number, amount, and type of beverage additives, HEAs exhibit unpredictable properties and results when their composition or type is altered, leading to a vast possible configurational space and their exceptional properties. This means that in a alloy system with certain principal elements, adjusting the amount of these elements can lead to the emergence of various properties and structures, resulting in properties that are entirely unexpected and diverse [ 57 ,  65 ,  66 – 67 ]. Furthermore, increasing the number of principal elements adds an additional degree of compositional freedom and complexity; such systems are nearly infinite [ 68 ]. Such flexibility also enables the engineerable characteristics and properties that can be adjusted based on design and industrial requirements. It should be noted that, unlike other three core effects, which are hypotheses, the cocktail effect is not a hypothesis and does not require proof [ 9 ]. According to Fig.  3 , the cocktail effect highlights how outstanding material properties of HEAs often result from unforeseen synergies. Similarly, other material behaviors, such as a near-zero thermal expansion coefficient or catalytic reactions, can also be viewed as the result of unpredictable, synergistic responses [ 9 ].

Alongside the well-established core effects that distinguish HEAs from conventional alloys, several characteristics can be seen as extensions or subsets of these core effects. These differences are depicted in Fig.  1 , where the properties and performance indicators along the arrow are shown to increase gradually from pure metals to HEAs. This highlights the enhanced capabilities that come from compositional complexity and synergistic effects in HEAs. It can be concluded that the properties of HEAs are not influenced by just one factor but are the result of the combined influence of four core effects working together. These synergistic effects enable HEAs to exhibit a combination of excellent mechanical, thermal, and functional properties beyond those of traditional alloys. All these core effects must be present; having only one is not enough. Despite many advances in the field of HEAs, the complex interaction between mechanisms remains not fully understood and predictable. Therefore, further research into the individual contribution of each mechanism and their interactions can help in designing and optimizing HEAs more effectively for specific engineering applications.

sections.heading: Phases and mechanical performance in HEAs
paragraphs: This section attempts to clarify the importance of deliberate compositional design, precise phase selection, and prediction in the development of HEAs. Choosing the appropriate phase structure must align with the intended service conditions and performance requirements. Without such strategies, balancing the cost, performance, and manufacturing processes for HEAs becomes difficult. Since much of the alloy’s behavior depends on the constituent phases, and design approaches focus on phase determination and prediction, understanding the atomic structures of HEAs and their related properties is highly beneficial for targeted design. Despite their complex composition, HEAs typically tend to form a single-phase solid solution (SS) with simple crystal lattices due to their high configurational entropy [ 74 ]. From the perspective of atomic structure in HEAs, alloying elements randomly occupy lattice sites as substitutional SS, allowing different atomic species to replace each other. As a result, the long-range periodicity of the crystal lattice gets disrupted [ 75 ]. Of course, these conditions are not incidental but rather result from the use of prediction tools, deliberate design, appropriate elemental selection, and suitable fabrication methods. The most common crystal structures in HEAs are FCC and BCC, with FCC appearing slightly more frequently than BCC. HEAs with an HCP structure are relatively rare because they lack the SS strengthening effect, caused by differences in atomic size and electronic structure among the elements, the high cost and rarity of some elements, limited applications, elemental compatibility issues, and phase segregation [ 76 ,  77 – 78 ]. Apart from these dominant crystal forms, more complex phases such as sigma, Laves, and FCC + BCC have also been observed in several HEAs systems [ 79 ].

According to Table  1 , HEAs that predominantly contain refractory elements in their compositions are classified as Refractory-HEAs with BCC structure, making them suitable for high-temperature applications. These alloys tend to be more expensive because their constituent elements are rarer and more costly than those required to form the FCC structure. HEAs with a BCC structure generally exhibit higher hardness and strength. Their high brittleness and low ductility at room temperature limit their application and necessitate structural modifications to improve ductility [ 79 ,  80 ]. In contrast, HEAs with FCC structures have gained significant attention due to their cheap and widely available constituent elements, excellent mechanical properties (including high ductility and formability resulting from various deformation mechanisms), and good phase stability. Additionally, these alloys offer manufacturing flexibility through various primary and secondary processes (such as rolling and ECAP), support a wide range of applications, and enable the potential to replace precious materials in applications like electrocatalysts. They also enable further improvements in strength and hardness through the use of suitable additives, while maintaining their inherent ductility [ 79 ,  81 ,  82 ]. When both BCC and FCC phases form in HEAs, the resulting structure typically leads to more varied mechanical behavior. Such mixed structures enhance yield strength, improve compressive strength, and maintain a moderate level of ductility [ 79 ,  83 ,  84 ]. The formation of intermetallic (IM) phases, such as Sigma and Laves, can result in a rougher microstructure [ 11 ], which increases local hardness but typically causes a significant decrease in overall ductility [ 79 ,  85 ,  86 ]. The mechanical properties of different phases in HEAs can be studied in detail in Ref. [ 38 ].

sections.heading: Applications of HEAs
paragraphs:
In recent years, significant research has been conducted on the design, phase prediction, and optimization of HEAs; however, research on the applications of these materials remains limited and scattered, and their development is still in the early stages. The final goal of developing these novel alloys is to exploit their exceptional potential for practical engineering and industrial applications; this potential has not yet been fully realized. It will require more attention and focus on future studies. Thanks to the unique combination of core effects and customizable phase structures and performance, HEAs have gained widespread recognition in various advanced engineering fields. Their properties, including high mechanical strength, acceptable ductility, thermal stability at high temperatures, excellent corrosion and oxidation resistance, and the ability to maintain phase integrity in harsh environments, make them suitable candidates for a wide range of applications. The use of HEAs has been expanded to encompass high-temperature structural components, wear-resistant coatings, aerospace components, nuclear sector applications, military applications, cryogenic systems, and electrical and energy-related applications. sections.heading: Processing routes of HEAs: effects on microstructure, phase evolution, and properties
paragraphs: This section attempts to clarify that, beyond alloy composition design and phase prediction, deliberate control over processing and fabrication methods is essential for engineering HEAs. To achieve a successful alloy design and preparation, it is essential to comprehend the manufacturing processes of HEAs, as well as the associated microstructural features and property outcomes, along with targeted microstructure, property considerations, and cost factors as part of the design process. Even with the same chemical compositions, variations in fabrication techniques can lead to different phase formations, ranging from crystalline to amorphous regions and various structures [ 9 ,  132 ,  133 – 134 ]. The selection of fabrication methods can directly affect phase transformations, stability, composition uniformity, phase separation, grain size, defect density, and dendritic structure, all of which influence the mechanical, thermal, and functional properties of the final HEA. For example, fabricating HEAs with the desired composition using Selective Laser Melting (SLM) and arc melting methods results in distinctly different structures and textures due to varying solidification conditions. The SLM method results in a Widmanstätten structure, whereas the arc melting method results in a dendritic structure. Moreover, HEAs produced through additive manufacturing methods exhibit better mechanical properties compared to those produced through casting methods, due to the high cooling rates and the associated reduction in grain size [ 135 ].

Besides the selection of the preparation method, adjusting processing parameters within a given technique can lead to significantly different alloy characteristics and outcomes. For instance, molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the different cooling rates of equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi HEA strongly influence phase evolution. A critical cooling rate of 2.5 × 10 10  K/s results in amorphous phase formation, which is linked to severe lattice distortion. Such rapid solidification inhibits crystallization and improves structural properties by increasing dislocation density and twinning-induced deformation [ 136 ]. Other research shows that processing an alloy using the SPS method under two different conditions, specifically, increasing the heating rate, results in higher mechanical properties due to reduced grain growth [ 137 ]. Despite the novelty of HEAs, the methods for fabricating HEAs are similar to those used for conventional alloys. Figure  4  presents the primary fabrication methods of HEAs, categorized by their processing state as solid-state, liquid-state, and vapor-phase routes, along with their related products and secondary operations. sections.heading: Liquid state processing (LSP)
paragraphs: In general, the liquid-state processing of HEAs involves the complete melting of the elements and their thorough mixing to achieve a uniform distribution at the atomic level. This method allows for adequate mixing but requires precise control over melting behavior, cooling rates, and atmosphere to avoid unwanted phases, phase separations, compositional loss, and impurities.

sections.heading: Conventional LSP methods
paragraphs: Heat sources for melting in conventional LSP include electric arc, induction, and resistive elements. The LSP manufacturing of HEAs, such as vacuum arc melting (VAM) [ 138 ], vacuum induction melting [ 139 ], and resistance furnace melting [ 140 ], are among the most common and straightforward methods for producing these materials, and during the early development of HEAs, casting and solidifying from the molten state were mainly used [ 2 ]. In these methods, different elements are combined in the molten state, and after cooling, the alloy’s final configuration forms. Typically, the process is conducted in a vacuum to prevent unwanted reactions with oxygen and to maintain the alloy’s proportions. Using a vacuum also increases homogeneity, reduces casting defects, and shortens heat treatment time [ 141 ]. The VAM technique, when performed in a controlled atmosphere, produces more uniform samples due to the stirring process. Key parameters in this process include: melt temperature, raw material purity, process atmosphere (vacuum, shielding gas, reducing gas), mold design and material (copper, ceramic, graphite, etc.), cooling rate, heat source power and type (arc, induction, resistive), melt stirring or agitation, cooling rate, potential for mold contamination, remelting cycles for uniform composition, and vacuum or pressure control. The main advantage of LSP methods is the ability to quickly and cost-effectively produce bulk alloys with precise compositions; however, disadvantages include casting defects (such as shrinkage, segregation, etc.), potential evaporation of elements with low melting points, formation of heterogeneous microstructures due to low cooling rates, dendritic microstructures, and challenges in achieving precise phase control, all of which can reduce mechanical properties [ 142 ]. Generally, liquid-state methods are suitable for the initial production and exploration of fundamental properties of HEAs. Still, to achieve stable microstructures and improved mechanical properties, it is necessary to optimize process parameters, combine with other techniques, or perform secondary operations [ 143 ]. One specific method in this category is the Bridgman solidification technique. The Bridgman method is a directional solidification technique that allows for columnar grain growth and the production of single-crystal HEAs via slow solidification in a controlled thermal gradient condition. This provides precise control over grain orientation and phase distribution. Key advantages of the Bridgman method include the ability to produce large crystals with minimal defects, oriented microstructures, and anisotropic properties [ 144 ]. However, its limitations include the requirement for time-consuming and expensive equipment with precise temperature control. Bridgman solidification has been successfully used for HEAs such as CoCrFeNiAl₀.₃ and AlCoCrFeNi [ 145 ,  146 ].

sections.heading: Advanced LSP methods
paragraphs: Additive manufacturing (AM) is categorized as an advanced manufacturing technique that offers new opportunities for the fabrication of HEAs. The heat sources in AM could be a high-power laser, an electron beam, or an electric arc. Well-known AM methods used in HEAs fabrication include selective laser melting [ 147 ], electron beam melting (first proposed by Fujieda et al. [ 148 ]), wire arc AM [ 149 ], and plasma arc melting. AM produces parts directly from a 3D digital model created using computer-aided design (CAD) technology, employing a layer-by-layer printing process. This method allows for building large-scale parts with complex geometries and internal features [ 150 ]. By enabling the fabrication of complex shapes, short lead times, and minimal post-processing, AM is very efficient for developing HEAs with detailed geometries and properties in specific applications. Furthermore, it provides design flexibility, rapid prototyping, and reduces raw material waste [ 151 ]. Additionally, the rapid cooling rate in this process stabilizes single-phase structures, such as FCC or BCC. It inhibits the formation of unwanted phases, resulting in fine-grained microstructures that enhance mechanical properties [ 79 ,  152 ]. Essential parameters in AM include the power of the energy source (laser, electron beam, or plasma arc), scanning speed or nozzle/beam movement, layer thickness, scanning strategy and path, nozzle-to-surface distance, substrate temperature or preheat, type and rate of shielding gas or ambient vacuum, material feed rate (powder or wire), and cooling rate between layers or different regions. However, challenges such as chemical composition heterogeneity, residual stresses, and cracks caused by rapid cooling and heating are essential considerations in the path to industrializing these alloys through additive manufacturing methods [ 153 ,  154 ]. Recent research shows that careful selection of process parameters, especially in techniques such as selective laser melting, can result in parts with excellent mechanical properties, high structural stability, and suitable thermal characteristics [ 150 ,  155 ,  156 ].

sections.heading: Solid state processing (SSP)
paragraphs: Advanced materials, such as HEAs, refer to materials that can be precisely engineered with the desired properties and characteristics through synthesis techniques and control of microstructure [ 157 ]. Although many early investigations on HEAs focused mainly on melting and solidification techniques, the increasing demand for advanced applications with precise structural requirements has gradually shifted attention toward SSP methods. Engineering and controlling the structure and composition of advanced materials are better achieved through processes that operate under non-equilibrium conditions. For this reason, SSP methods such as mechanical alloying (MA) have gained significant attention from researchers [ 158 ]. The main advantages of SSP lie in their ability to provide better control over phase formation and microstructure evolution, while reducing the formation of unwanted and segregated phases, which are often seen in LSP. In SSP, the processing temperature is generally maintained below the melting point of the constituent elements, allowing for the formation of more uniform and stable SS phases [ 134 ]. From a process standpoint, SSP of HEAs can be viewed as similar to powder metallurgy (PM). This is because the main steps, (1) powder production, (2) powder mixing and alloying, (3) powder compaction and shaping, and (4) sintering are entirely consistent with PM framework methods. Powder production can be achieved through various techniques, including gas or water atomization, mechanical milling, or chemical processes. The mixed elements powder is then compacted into a mold to create a part known as the "Green Part", which has the desired shape but lacks adequate mechanical strength. The density of the green part, known as green part density, significantly impacts the density and porosity of the final component. Since density and strength are generally closely related, a higher green part density results in a denser part with better mechanical properties. The final step, sintering, is a heat treatment process that forms metallurgical bonding between powder particles. This process significantly reduces porosity, yielding a dense bulk part with acceptable mechanical properties, strength, and structural integrity [ 159 ]. Given the many advantages that HEAs fabrication techniques provide through SSP, the issues related to this discussion will be examined in detail.

sections.heading: Mechanical alloying (MA)
paragraphs: MA is one of the most important SSP for producing HEAs, which are used as inputs for fabricating bulk parts after sintering. John Benjamin [ 160 ] developed this method in the mid-1960s. In MA, mixtures of pure elemental powders are alloyed in a chamber with sufficient mechanical energy (such as a planetary ball mill or shaker) under the influence of intense and repeated balls impacts. The MA process involves repeated cold welding, fracturing, and rewelding of powder particles, resulting in the formation of alloy phases. Unlike melting, where the energy required to create the desired structure and phase is applied thermally to the system, in the MA method, the energy required for alloying is introduced mechanically into the system [ 161 ]. The main advantages of MA include precise control over composition and microstructure, preservation of unstable phases (metastable phases), and the ability to process at low temperatures. In this method, there is a possibility of powder contamination from abrasive particles and the chamber wall, as well as oxidation of the particles, especially during long process times. The importance of MA in producing HEAs can be summarized as follows [ 134 ,  161 ,  162 ]: No need to melt:  The MA process is carried out below the melting temperature, which helps prevent unwanted phase formation and separation, and recrystallization. Production of nano and amorphous structures:  Due to high energy input and intense strain, it is possible to produce alloys with ultra fine-grained (UFG), nanocrystalline, or even amorphous structures, resulting in enhanced mechanical properties. Preparation of metastable phases:  Many phases that cannot form under equilibrium conditions are fabricated during the MA process. Combining refractory or incompatible elements:  MA enables alloying between elements that tend to separate in the molten state. Precise control of chemical composition:  By controlling the ratio of incoming powders, the final composition can be adjusted. Possibility of mass production on an industrial scale Possibility of combining with various sintering methods

The parameters of the MA process greatly influence the quality of alloying. For example, when the speed is excessive, the balls tend to stick to the wall due to centrifugal force, and practically no alloying occurs. Besides, high speed increases contamination and heat production. Since a large amount of mechanical energy is converted into heat, the temperature rise in the chamber becomes particularly critical, especially in nanocrystal production. With intense milling, increased dynamic recrystallization leads to larger crystal sizes and a reduction in internal strain [ 163 ]. sections.heading: Conventional sintering
paragraphs: In the Fabrication of HEAs by conventional sintering methods, such as cold pressing (CP), pressureless sintering (PS) [ 165 ], metal powders with the desired chemical composition are first prepared through MA. Then, the powder is heated in a controlled atmosphere, such as a vacuum or an inert gas, without applying external pressure during the sintering process. The final density of the part is usually lower than that achieved with advanced techniques. Generally, Conventional sintering methods have simple equipment and lower cost. Nevertheless, due to the slow diffusion and the possibility of forming unwanted phases, careful control of temperature, sintering time, and powder composition is crucial to achieve a uniform microstructure and desirable mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Advanced sintering
paragraphs: Recently, the combined use of MA and advanced sintering techniques, such as hot pressing (HP-semi advanced) [ 166 ], hot isostatic pressing (HIP) [ 167 ], hot oscillating pressing (HOP) [ 168 ], and microwave sintering (MS) [ 169 ], and spark plasma sintering (SPS) has been widely employed in fabricating and densifying HEAs due to its numerous advantages. These methods differ fundamentally in how heat is applied; along with pressure, heat can be supplied by electric current (in SPS), a resistance furnace (in HIP, HP), or microwave waves (in MS). These methods significantly shorten processing time, are energy-efficient, maintain the original powder structure, and even enable the production of bulk parts with nanostructures. Furthermore, advanced sintering methods produce a highly uniform microstructure and element distribution, prevent excessive grain growth, reduce porosity, and provide very high densities. All of which contribute to enhanced mechanical properties [ 170 ].

Reviewing the literature shows that HEAs produced by MA + SPS are among the most common fabrication methods, especially when nanocrystalline structures and high densification are required. [ 134 ]. SPS, also known as the field-assisted sintering technique (FAST) or pulsed electric current sintering (PECS), is regarded as one of the most effective methods for fabricating HEAs. In the SPS process, uniaxial pressure is applied to consolidate the powder, while a pulsed electric current is simultaneously used to generate heat via the Joule heating mechanism. The improved thermal efficiency of SPS primarily stems from its unique heating mechanism. According to Fig.  5 , Pulsed direct current flows through components such as punches, spacers, the die, and the powder compact, thereby generating heat internally due to the electrical resistance of the material. In contrast, conventional sintering depends on external heating sources. The final microstructure and properties of the sintered sample can be adjusted by changing parameters such as current density, applied pressure, dwell temperature, dwell time, pulse pattern, and cooling rate [ 171 ,  172 ,  173 ,  174 ,  175 ,  176 ,  177 – 178 ]. Figure 5 Schematic of a spark plasma sintering device for the fabrication of high entropy alloys.

sections.heading: Gas state processing
paragraphs: Methods for producing HEAs in the gas phase, such as physical vapor deposition (PVD), including magnetron sputtering [ 190 ] and pulsed laser deposition (PLD) [ 191 ], chemical vapor deposition (CVD) [ 128 ], molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) [ 192 ], or atomic layer deposition [ 193 ], are used to fabricate thin films and surface coatings. In these processes, different elements are deposited onto the substrate in atomic or ionic form from the gas phase, and a random combination forms the final structure [ 194 ,  195 ]. Electrochemical methods are also used to produce thin films of HEAs. Yao et al. [ 196 ] prepared BiFeCoNiMn HEA via an electrochemical process. The primary advantages of gas-state processing of HEAs include precise control over the chemical composition and thickness of the layers and the opportunity to investigate the surface properties of the alloys. However, its disadvantages include limited volume production, high cost, and the requirement for advanced vacuum equipment. Overall, gas methods are highly suitable for fundamental research, creating resistant coatings, and studying the surface properties of HEAs. However, for the industrial production of bulk parts, they should be combined with other methods. This technique is especially beneficial for developing wear-resistant coatings, particularly on Medical and industrial parts [ 197 ]. Due to the excellent biocompatibility of some HEAs and their very suitable surface properties in physiological environments, the use of gas-phase coating is common in improving surface properties. It should be noted that gas-phase processing methods are more expensive than other methods in terms of operating and equipment costs [ 198 ,  199 ].

sections.heading: Welding processing
paragraphs:
Welding HEAs involves scientific challenges and unique opportunities due to their multi-principal element compositions and complex phase stability. Recent research shows that many HEAs can be effectively welded using fusion and solid-state methods, if phase transformations, elemental segregation, and thermal gradients are carefully controlled. Techniques such as laser beam welding (LBW) and electron beam welding (EBW) enable localized fusion with precise heat input. Still, they can also cause phase decomposition or reduce hardness in the fusion zone [ 200 ]. In contrast, solid-state welding (SSW) techniques, such as friction stir welding (FSW) and diffusion bonding (DB), provide better grain refinement and phase retention, thereby reducing thermal-induced defects. The use of these methods on alloys like AlCoCrFeNi and CoCrFeNiAl₀.₃ includes detailed evaluations of weld microstructures, mechanical integrity, and heat-affected zones, confirming the feasibility of welding HEAs [ 201 ,  202 – 203 ]. Details of solid-state welding methods for HEAs, including their advantages and disadvantages, as well as the effects of each technique on the microstructure and phase transitions, are thoroughly discussed in Ref. sections.heading: Techno-economic assessment of HEAs raw materials and processing routes
paragraphs: This section discusses the economic aspects related to the design and fabrication of HEAs. The main focus is on two axes: first, the cost and availability of alloying elements, and second, the economic evaluation of the different process routes. The aim is to achieve more cost-effective and industrially viable choices in the design and fabrication of HEAs by a detailed assessment of these subjects.

sections.heading: Cost and abundance of raw materials
paragraphs: Besides designing and fabrication of HEAs, it is essential to consider their technical and economic aspects. One major challenge in bringing these advanced materials to commercialization and mass production is choosing elements based on cost and availability. The element selection HEAs determines not only their properties and performance but also their economic viability and scalability. HEAs include some expensive metals or rare-earth elements, which can significantly increase production costs and complicate fabrication. Therefore, efforts to replace costly elements with more affordable metals or use an alternative preparation method are vital for the economical and sustainable growth of these alloys. Such an approach is feasible in HEAs while maintaining phase stability, properties, and performance comparable to those of more costly alternatives.

It is crucial to develop HEAs with cost-effective elements to facilitate the transition from laboratory to industrial scale. The elements such as Fe, Mn, Cr, and Al are favored for cost-effective HEAs due to their low cost and high abundance. In contrast, elements such as Nb, Ta, W, and Hf are associated with high commodity prices and supply risks, although they offer superior mechanical and thermal properties. Furthermore, limited global reserves and high extraction costs of certain elements make the large-scale production of HEAs with specific elements that have no substitutes economically challenging. A striking example of geography-based supply chains is the global reliance on China’s rare earth element (REE) industry, which now holds both reserves and production capacity. China’s inventory of rare earth elements ranks first in the world, with an approximately 37–50% share of global reserves and over 69% share of global mine production, as well as almost 90% of global refinery capacity by 2023 [ 224 ,  225 ]. This concentration has created a critical supply bottleneck, especially for high-tech sectors such as electronics, renewable energy, and defense. In line with this discussion and further clarification, Gorsse et al. introduced a valuable and comprehensive sustainability database, 18 key elements used in HEAs across indicators, including raw material price, supply risk, embodied energy, and human rights pressure [ 226 ]. This dataset helps alloy designers to benchmark compositions in terms of their performance as well as economic and ethical metrics, promoting reasonable element selection.

To reduce the cost of raw materials in the production of HEAS, several methods have been proposed. In this regard, Hariharan and Sivaprasad [ 227 ] have introduced a technique called “Alloy Mixing” for the synthesis of HEAs using alloy scraps. They investigated the feasibility of this method by producing a nearly equiatomic CrCuFeMnNi alloy on a laboratory scale. In this process, scraps including 304L stainless steel, Nichrome 80, and electrical-grade copper were collected from various sources and melted in a vacuum arc furnace. Additionally, to fine-tune the final composition, amounts of Mn and Cr elements were added to the mixture. The results showed that the alloy obtained through alloy mixing has a microstructure similar to that of an alloy with the same composition produced from pure elements. More importantly, they reported that the costs associated with manufacturing this alloy were reduced by approximately nine times per kilogram compared to using pure raw materials. From a mechanical properties perspective, an increase of about 50% in yield strength compared to using pure raw materials was reported, which was attributed to the presence of some impurities (especially Si) and the solid solution strengthening, which can be considered as a clear result of the synergy of the cocktail effect. However, it is emphasized that the type, amount, and precise control of the impurities strongly influence the final properties. If the amount of impurities is not properly managed, the desired properties may be compromised. This approach could provide an efficient solution for the mass and low-cost production of HEAs, provided that the composition and process control are carefully observed. Another approach is to use less expensive elements in some applications instead of more costly ones. It is reported that, in the CrMnFeCoNi alloy system, substituting Co with Fe can significantly lower material costs while maintaining phase stability [ 228 ]. In other research, it is reported instead of using costly elements to improve strength, adding Al, which is low-cost and low-density, can increase the strength of the alloy in some cases [ 229 ]. This approach can be investigated for other cases based on performance. In some cases, developing HEAs made from cheaper, more accessible elements with similar applications and performance as more expensive alloys is possible. For instance, in electrocatalytic applications, transition metals such as Fe, Co, and Ni can potentially replace with precious metals [ 230 ,  231 – 232 ]. Additionally, developing and investigating alloys like iron-based HEAs, which have high potential for industrialization [ 225 ], could help reduce HEAs production costs.

paragraphs:
Despite the significant advantages of HEAs and great potential for industrial applications, their manufacturing costs remain challenging. Different synthesis methods have substantial differences in terms of energy consumption, equipment requirements, and scalability. Economic evaluation of these methods not only aids in better decision-making for choosing the production route but also plays a key role in attracting investors and driving industrial development. Especially in industrial and research projects, cost and economic efficiency analysis can pave the way for the sustainable development of HEAs and prevent waste of resources. Therefore, including economic evaluation in HEA studies is not only recommended but also essential for their operational and commercial success. sections.heading: High entropy alloys design
paragraphs:
In HEAs, compositional design is the decisive lever for stabilizing desired solid-solution phases and avoiding detrimental intermetallics and phases. If the alloy composition is not properly designed, the alloy synthesis will fail [ 233 ]. Designing HEAs through experimentation, which involves trial and error, is both costly and time-consuming [ 38 ]. With different goals, such as Composition [ 234 ], microstructure [ 235 ], or property design [ 236 ], various computational tools, such as Density Functional Theory (DFT) [ 237 ], Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation [ 238 ], phase diagram calculation (CALPHAD) [ 239 ], etc., have been widely used to design HEAs. Table  9  provides an overview of the primary design strategies of HEAs. These methods range from empirical rules and experimental synthesis to advanced computational and data-driven techniques. Each approach offers unique advantages and faces specific limitations, depending on the purpose of the analysis, underlying assumptions, input data, time, and cost considerations. According to Table  9 , a synergistic integration of these methods, leveraging both computational accuracy and experimental validation, has become an increasingly adopted strategy in HEA design workflows.
 Table 9 Design methods for High Entropy Alloys: A Review of Principles, Benefits, and Drawbacks Method Brief description Advantages Disadvantages Reference Experimental Design Classical approach involving actual alloy synthesis and property evaluation Provides real and reliable results, allowing complete control over synthesis parameters and enabling real-world validation Expensive and time-consuming, with a limited number of compositions that can be tested in each experiment [ 242 ,  249 ] Empirical Rules (Phase formation rules) Use of criteria like thermodynamic and Hume-Rothery to predict Phase and solid solution formation Understandable, very fast, and easy; it does not require complex calculations and helps in the initial screening of compositions Limited accuracy; Inability to predict performance properties, [ 4 ,  11 ,  242 ,  250 ] Machine Learning Data-driven models trained on datasets to predict HEAs properties or phase formation Extremely fast once trained, allowing for efficient exploration of the vast compositional space of combinations Requires large and high-quality datasets; vulnerable to overfitting; poor generalization to unseen compositions. Low interpretability [ 240 ,  251 ,  252 ,  253 – 254 ] CALPHAD A thermodynamic modeling approach that uses assessed databases and Gibbs energy functions to predict phase equilibria in multicomponent systems Effective phase stability predictions with minimizing Gibbs energy, enabling temperature-dependent phase analysis, and integrating well with experimental and DFT data Accuracy depends on the quality of existing databases. Limited data for many HEA compositions, less effective for non-equilibrium or metastable phases [ 255 ,  256 – 257 ] Miedema Model Semi-empirical method for estimating mixing enthalpies using macroscopic atom theory and tabulated atomic parameters Very fast, easy to use for initial thermodynamic screening; no need for quantum calculations Low accuracy; ignores crystallographic and bonding details; Limited to predicting formation enthalpy [ 258 ,  259 ] AB Initio Molecular Dynamics (AIMD) Quantum-based molecular dynamics simulations to study behavior at the atomic scale using DFT-derived forces Very accurate, providing atomistic insight into the real dynamic behavior of atoms, making it best for exploring novel HEAs. It also provides atomistic-level details of the alloys time-consuming and computationally intensive; limited to small supercells, not suitable for examining all the complexities of HEAs [ 4 ,  75 ,  260 ] Density Functional Theory (DFT) First-principles quantum mechanics method to calculate the total energy and electronic structure of materials High accuracy for structural and electronic predictions, making it suitable for stability and bonding studies High computational cost: System size limitations do not directly account for temperature or entropy effects [ 261 ,  262 ] Monte Carlo Simulation Statistical method using stochastic sampling to explore atomic configurations and thermodynamic properties of disordered alloys Suitable for configurational entropy and phase stability analysis; useful in modeling disordered systems Computation-heavy for large complex systems; sensitive to input parameters; limited to thermodynamic (equilibrium) properties [ 263 ,  264 ] High-Throughput Screening (HTS) Automated evaluation of thousands of possible alloy compositions using either computational models (e.g., CALPHAD/DFT) or experimental combinatorial techniques Enables rapid discovery across large composition spaces; both computational and experimental HTS show promising results Requires extensive data, resources, and infrastructure; High-throughput experiments may be limited in scale and property measurements [ 11 ,  265 ,  266 ]

Although methods such as DFT, AIMD, and HTS are practical and widely used in HEAs design, their application is limited by high costs, time-consuming calculations, and uncertainty in the results [ 240 ]. One of the most widely used methods for designing HEAs is the use of empirical rules, which are related to the subject of the present work. One of the main focuses in the design of HEAs, which has been of interest from the early days of HEAs, has been the identification of possible phases and structures, determining SS compositions and stabilizing them, based on empirical rules [ 38 ]. Empirical rules approaches are much faster, simpler, and helpful in selecting HEAs compositions, accelerating screening, and reducing design cost and time [ 38 ,  54 ]. The widely adopted empirical parameter rules offer valuable guidance for predicting phase formation in HEAs. Nevertheless, the predictive accuracy of these models is still limited, with the best-performing approaches achieving only around 72% accuracy [ 241 ]. Therefore, experimental validation remains essential to confirm the reliability of such predictions [ 242 ]. Empirical rules can be classified into three categories [ 38 ]: Calculations related to thermodynamic rules using entropy of mixing, enthalpy of mixing, and alloy melting temperature [ 243 ,  244 ,  245 – 246 ]. Calculations related to Hume-Rothery rules based on the atomic size mismatch, valence electron concentration, and electronegativity [ 245 ,  246 – 247 ]. Design criteria based on lattice distortion [ 248 ]

Before delving into the details of design based on empirical and phase formation rules, a section entitled element selection is presented. This section serves as the input to the design process. It outlines the effects of each element on phase characteristics, as well as on the properties and performance of the final alloy.

sections.heading: Element selection
paragraphs:
In designing HEAs and selecting their constituent components, in addition to relying on the design strategies and experimental knowledge that will be discussed following, the cocktail effect can be strategically employed. Based on the concept of interactions among elements, the phase constitution and microstructure of the alloy can be tailored by utilizing appropriate elements. The selection of elements has a profound influence on the performance of HEAs. Within the vast composition space of HEAs, the chemical nature of the elements, atomic size, electronic configuration, and interactions among alloying elements have a determining influence on not only the potential phases and their stability, e.g., FCC, BCC, HCP, or intermetallic compounds, but also the ensuing mechanical, thermal, and chemical response. Furthermore, the performance of the alloy is affected by its size, distribution, and synergistic interactions between phases. Insights into each element’s role enable more targeted and efficient alloy design, particularly when the goal is to optimize specific properties, such as hardness, strength, corrosion resistance, or high-temperature stability. For instance, some elements promote ductility and phase stability, whereas others enhance hardness or confer refractory characteristics. Table  10  presents an overview of the possible effects that individual elements may exert on the microstructure and properties of HEAs. Some non-metallic elements have also been identified as minor alloying additions in HEAs, offering potential for incorporation into other alloy systems. These elements could be evaluated to determine their effects on structural and functional properties in other HEA configurational systems.
 Table 10 Possible effects of key elements in HEAs on phase formation and material properties Element Possible effects Reference Al Al additions convert FCC structures to BCC phases and enhance solid-solution strengthening. At high Al content, brittle intermetallic phases form, increasing hardness and wear resistance but reducing ductility [ 10 ,  267 ] Fe Fe with ferromagnetic properties increases solid solution strengthening and yield strength in HEAs [ 10 ,  267 ] Ni Ni stabilizes FCC solid solutions and improves ductility and toughness. It also enhances corrosion resistance and lowers stacking-fault energy in CoCrFeMnNi-type HEAs [ 10 ,  267 ] Cu It promotes the formation of the FCC phase, which tends to segregate within the intergranular regions and may lead to the precipitation of Cu-rich spherical nanophases, thereby enhancing the overall mechanical performance of the high-entropy alloy [ 10 ] Zr It may lead to the formation of intermetallic compounds, which can adversely affect the strength and ductility of the HAEs [ 10 ] Co Co strongly promotes single-phase FCC solid solutions (with Fe and Ni) in HEAs, and a small amount of its addition yields alloys with excellent ductility, wear resistance, and toughness. In addition, it prevents the alloy from breaking when it cools [ 10 ,  267 ] Cr Cr with intrinsic ferromagnetic properties forms stable passive oxide films, significantly enhancing corrosion and oxidation resistance. It also stabilizes BCC phases at high content, contributing to high-temperature strength [ 10 ,  267 ] Ti Due to its large atomic radius, Ti introduces lattice distortion and promotes a higher content of HCP/BCC phases. Moderate Ti raises strength and hardness via solid-solution and ordered precipitation; excess Ti yields brittle intermetallics [ 10 ,  267 ]–[ 269 ] V V is a refractory element that significantly boosts hardness and wear resistance but reduces ductility. It may promote high-temperature strength [ 268 ,  269 – 270 ] W W is a heavy refractory that substantially hardens HEAs by solid-solution strengthening. It gives exceptional high-temperature strength and hardness [ 268 ,  269 ,  271 ,  272 ] Nb Nb raises hardness and wear resistance. It stabilizes BCC (and laves) phases, boosting high-temperature strength and creep resistance [ 268 ,  269 ,  273 ,  274 – 275 ] Mo Mo is a refractory element that greatly increases hardness and wear resistance. This section highlights how various commonly used elements influence phase formation, thermodynamic behavior, and key performance characteristics. These insights provide a foundational basis for more effective HEA design and the precise tailoring of alloy properties.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic rules
paragraphs: Numerous studies recommend that, before starting experimental procedures, a thorough investigation of possible phase formations and identifying optimal combinations be conducted in HEA design [ 244 ,  284 ,  285 – 286 ]. The crystal structure of HEAs has a significant influence on their mechanical and physical properties [ 9 ,  39 ]. Experimental studies have confirmed that, with precise compositional design, these alloys typically tend to form FCC or BCC SS, rather than evolving into IM or complex multiphase structures, an outcome attributed to their high mixing entropy [ 2 ,  287 ]. Recent advancements in HEAs have clarified the importance of understanding fundamental thermodynamic principles and phase stability criteria for effective alloy design. Some HEAs systems can display IM phases or amorphous structures under specific conditions, but research mainly focuses on developing single-phase SS. This preference is related to the excellent mechanical performance and improved functional properties of these alloys compared to conventional alloys [ 2 ,  38 ,  41 ,  288 ,  289 ]. It has been reported that when HEAs form solid solutions with only BCC or FCC structures, the strength and ductility are greatly improved [ 267 ].

sections.heading: Gibbs free energy
paragraphs: However, due to the computational complexity involved in assessing all potential phases in multicomponent systems, a simplified evaluative approach is often favored [ 244 ,  294 ]. Research has shown that the enthalpy of mixing (ΔH mix ) and the entropic term (T m . ΔS mix ) in Eq. ( 2 ) contribute differently to SS formation, which will be explored in the following sections. Despite the simplicity and speed of this method, it’s most important limitation is the inability to predict complex phases in HEAS, such as intermetallic Laves and Sigma phases. However, it is a effective, fast and low cost method for predicting FCC and BCC single-phase solid solutions [ 297 ].

sections.heading: Entropic term: entropy of mixing and alloy melting temperature (T m ·ΔS mix )
paragraphs: In HEAs design, the acceptable range of ΔS mix  is equal to or greater than 1.5R (about 12.47 to 17.5 J K −1  mol −1 ) [ 247 ]. Figure  6  illustrates the varying magnitudes of alloy entropy based on the mixing entropy of the alloys. HEAs can be seen as an extension of low-entropy alloys (LEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) [ 4 ,  245 ]. Unlike conventional alloys, HEAs exhibit complex structural configurations and unique properties, which are attributed to high entropy in their systems, features that often fall outside the capabilities of traditional and classical alloy design principles. HEAs are conceptualized based on the principle that an increase in configurational entropy can significantly reduce the system’s Gibbs free energy (according to Eq.  2 ). The high mixing entropy enhances atomic randomness within the crystal lattice, thereby reducing the tendency toward phase segregation or the formation of ordered structures. The stabilized SS is very strong due to high entropy, and it is not possible to distinguish which atom is the solute and which is the solvent [ 244 ]. This entropic effect becomes more pronounced at elevated temperatures, further promoting the formation of stable SS [ 9 ]. Consequently, a high value of ΔS mix  emerges as a key indicator of the thermodynamic driving force for SS formation. When equal atomic fractions are applied to the constituent elements in an alloy, the entropy of mixing reaches its maximum value. Consequently, multi-principal element alloy systems with equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions exhibit significantly higher mixing entropy compared to conventional binary or ternary alloys. Figure 6 Schematic diagram of alloy classification.

Figure  7  displays the configurational entropy of equiatomic alloy systems as furcation of number of elements. Alloys are categorized into low, medium, and high entropy classifications based on their entropy values, which correspond to the number of elements. As mentioned, an increase in the number of elements results in a rise in configurational entropy [ 4 ,  299 ]. Figure 7 Effect of the number of equiatomic elements on the mixing entropy of the system.

Given that both temperature (T m ) and entropy change (ΔS mix ) are inherently positive in the entropic term, a high entropy of mixing helps to lower the overall Gibbs free energy. This reduction provides a thermodynamic driving force for the formation of an SS [ 244 ]. Therefore, compounds that might tend to phase separate or form intermetallics at room temperature can become stable solid solutions at elevated temperatures.

sections.heading: Enthalpy of mixing (ΔH mix )
paragraphs: Unlike the entropic term (T m . ΔS mix ), which is inherently positive, the enthalpy of mixing can exhibit either positive or negative values, depending on the interactions among the constituent elements. Numerous studies indicate that both the sign and magnitude of ΔH mix  influence phase stability. In binary alloy systems, a negative ΔHmix typically indicates the possibility of IM compound formation. Conversely, a positive mixing enthalpy often results in miscibility gaps within the liquid phase, restricting the solubility of the constituent elements in their solid form. This behavior is also observable in HEAs; however, the inclusion of multiple elements adds further thermodynamic complexities. When ΔH mix  is significantly negative, it indicates strong interatomic bonding, which facilitates the formation of IM compounds. In contrast, a significantly positive ΔH mix  generally leads to poor miscibility of the elements, raising the chances of phase separation or compositional partitioning [ 244 ].

Notably, regardless of whether the value is positive or negative, a large absolute magnitude of ΔH mix  generally inhibits the formation of SS. When ΔH mix  is near zero, atoms of different elements tend to distribute randomly within the crystal lattice, which enhances the stability of a single-phase SS. Therefore, the absolute value of mixing enthalpy can be viewed as a quantitative measure of a system’s resistance to forming an SS. This assessment shows that extreme values of enthalpy, whether highly negative or highly positive, act as barriers to the formation of uniform SS phases [ 244 ]. To obtain SS HEAs, the ΔH mix  value should be adjusted in the range of − 15 to 5 kJ mol −1  [ 247 ].

Considering Eq. ( 7 ), Ω is inherently positive and must exceed a critical threshold to promote SS formation. If the entropic contribution outweighs ΔH mix  (i.e., Ω > 1), SS formation is thermodynamically favored. Conversely, if Ω < 1, IM compounds or phase segregation are likely to occur before SS stabilization in the alloy system; in other words, the probability of forming an SS phase increases with an omega value greater than 1. Thus, Ω functions as a reliable predictive metric for evaluating the tendency of an alloy to form SS. A meaningful relationship exists between high-temperature stability and Gibbs free energy. Stability at room temperature (for room temperature applications) means that, at 298 K, the composition/phase with the minimum ΔG is favored. High-temperature stability (for high-temperature applications) refers to the phase with the lowest ΔG at a specific temperature (e.g., 1000–1500 K). Because changing temperature can reorder the stability ranking of phases.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic–processing coupling in HEAs
paragraphs: The mixing free energy (ΔG mix ) governs key aspects of HEAs’ behavior, serving as a fundamental parameter for tailoring properties through strategic composition selection and optimized processing. By deliberately tuning ΔG mix , engineers can optimize the alloy’s microstructure to achieve desirable mechanical, thermal, and functional characteristics for specific applications. HEAs generally remain stable as single-component solution phases at high temperatures due to high configurational entropy but often decompose into lower-energy phases (such as intermetallics) as the temperature decreases. In other words, what is stable at high temperatures (usually due to the prominent role of the T.ΔS term) may be metastable and subject to decomposition at room temperature. For example, calculations show that in a five-element HEA, ΔS mix ≃1.6R and at 1000 K, T.ΔS≈0.14 eV/atom, the free energy of formation of many binary intermetallics is typically more negative than −0.3 eV/atom. Consequently, below about 1000 K, these intermetallics become more stable and overshadow the alloy solid solution phase of HEAs [ 302 ]. Therefore, some HEAs that exhibit single-phase solid solutions when synthesized at elevated temperatures via methods such as casting or LSP may be thermodynamically metastable at room temperature. This highlights the advantage of techniques like MA + SPS, which can produce low-temperature-stabilized single-phase HEAs or metastable HEAs that become stable at high temperatures. The fabrication route (e.g., rapid casting, mechanical alloying, SPS) also determines the resultant phase; consequently, the equilibrium state, defined by the minimum ΔG, may differ from the phase composition actually obtained under practical processing conditions [ 303 ]. In fact, as the process deviates from equilibrium conditions due to non-equilibrium factors such as high cooling rates, quenching, and slow diffusion, the phase predictions become less reliable. Therefore, in addition to design, selecting the correct processing route has a substantial impact on the phase and functional results. The kinetics of the process are also important. Even if a phase is minimal in terms of ΔG, kinetic pathways (such as slow diffusion or an activation energy barrier) may prevent rapid equilibrium from being reached; as a result, metastable phases may form or remain in the process. HEAs are known to exhibit sluggish diffusion, which can enhance this effect. Of course, the opposite point can also be considered. Since HEAs have sluggish diffusion, this restricts phase transformations in these materials and can help stabilize the solid solution phase [ 304 ].

sections.heading: Hume-rothery rules
paragraphs: In the previous section, thermodynamic criteria were discussed to promote the formation of a solid solution. However, these criteria do not always guarantee the best outcomes. Studies have shown that, in addition to thermodynamic factors, several other factors, including atomic size difference, electronegativity difference, and Valence electron concentration, also influence both phase formation and the mechanical properties of alloys. Additionally, Valence electron concentration serves as a useful empirical factor that can predict, with acceptable accuracy, the type of alloy structure.

In addition to influencing solid-solution formation, atomic size differences have been shown to significantly impact the mechanical properties and microstructural evolution of the HEAs. In line with this issue, Wu et al. [ 306 ] investigated the grain growth and mechanical properties behavior of CoCrFeMnNi, Al 0.2 CoCrFeMnNi, and Al 0.3 CoCrCu 0.3 FeNi alloys. All alloys mentioned have an FCC structure. Adding Al with a 0.2 molar ratio to CoCrFeMnNi increases the atomic size difference from 1.18% to 2.77%, resulting in a higher activation energy for grain growth in Al 0.2 CoCrFeMnNi compared to CoCrFeMnNi (rising from 325 to 434.4 kJ/mol). Al 0.3 CoCrCu0.3FeNi, with an atomic size difference of 3.65%, exhibits an activation energy of 761.3 kJ/mol for grain growth, which is higher than that of the previous two alloys. The lattice distortion in Al0.3CoCrCu0.3FeNi is much more significant than in CoCrFeMnNi. Additionally, Al0.3CoCrCu0.3FeNi exhibits better mechanical properties than CoCrFeMnNi under similar conditions, due to high lattice distortion and the pinning effect on dislocations caused by the substantial atomic size difference in these HEAs.
