paragraphs: The effect of VEC on phase formation in the mentioned ranges is a bit complex and not entirely clear, and is mostly an inference based on experimental results [ 308 ]. It should be noted that although the VEC value is helpful in predicting phase formation, it is not entirely reliable and must be used in conjunction with other rules in the HEAs design process.

The reported range for this parameter is below 0.175, which results in a stable SS. However, values exceeding this threshold may lead to covalent or ionic bonding tendencies, thereby facilitating the formation of IM or ordered phases [ 312 ,  313 ].

sections.heading: Light-weight HEAs and theoretical density of alloy
Challenges
paragraphs: Despite extensive research and progress made in the realm of HEAs, many fundamental challenges remain unresolved. The unique characteristics of HEAs, which are related to their compositional complexity and core effects, lead to challenges in precise alloy design, phase prediction, and processing. Addressing these challenges is the step that will carry HEAs research materials into practical solutions for the demands of various industries.

Complexity and overlap of core effects in HEAs: A barrier to predictive design The four core effects frame our understanding of HEA behavior, but their interplay remains poorly understood. The cocktail effect with complex and nonlinear synergy among alloying elements complicates the interpretation of structure–property relationships [ 63 ]. Overlap and simultaneity obscure individual roles, hindering the decoupling and quantification of their respective roles. Targeted studies are needed to dissect these interactions. Such clarity would refine design methods, speed up the development of HEAs, and support HEAs with predictable, optimized performance in structural and functional applications [ 320 ].

Complexity in phase prediction and lack of phase diagrams Unlike traditional alloys, which are designed based on binary and ternary phase diagrams, HEAs lack comprehensive and reliable high-order phase data. This limitation restricts the accurate design of compositions and phase stability predictions, making the development of HEAs with target properties a challenging task. Without a specific framework or comprehensive phase diagrams, the design process remains mainly empirical and trial-and-error [ 249 ]. Methods such as CALPHAD and machine learning have attempted to fill this gap, but the available databases severely limit their accuracy [ 321 ,  322 ].

High production cost and scalability issues Due to the vast compositional space and the lack of reliable predictive tools, most HEA compositions are still primarily discovered through empirical methods and trial-and-error experiments, which are costly and time-consuming. Experimental validation is required for designed alloys [ 242 ]. The cost of manufacturing for the development of these materials still faces serious challenges. Most research has led to the production of laboratory samples and has not reached mass production [ 323 ]. The relatively high cost of raw materials (especially refractory or rare-earth elements) compared with high-strength and austenitic stainless steels [ 324 ] and expensive processing methods (e.g., sputtering, powder metallurgy, etc.) make large-scale production economically challenging. Of course, HEAs are still in the early stages of development in economic aspects; steps have been taken in this direction. Ongoing efforts to optimize production methods and reduce costs show promising progress. Preparation of raw materials from scraps and waste, as well as fabrication using casting, seems very promising.

Processing and microstructural control challenges The selection of the appropriate processing route has a significant impact on the final mechanical properties and microstructure. Some alloy compositions are theoretically predicted to be achievable, but in practice, they are difficult to process (i.e., uncertainty in prediction and failure in processing) [ 325 ]. Processes like additive manufacturing and laser cladding often result in defects, element segregation, and cracks, limiting microstructural control and uniformity [ 326 ,  327 – 328 ]. Methods such as spark plasma sintering (SPS) produce finer microstructures and higher hardness compared to arc melting but require optimization. Processes with high tempeartures cause phase changes, dynamic recovery, and recrystallization, and in some cases, precise microstructure control is difficult [ 329 ]. The mechanical route, coupled with contamination, can lead to the formation of unwanted secondary phases that negatively affect the final properties [ 330 ].

Lack of standardization and industrial qualification Unlike conventional alloys, HEAs lack established industrial standards, performance testing methods, and certification pathways necessary for industrial integration [ 39 ,  331 ]. For many HEAs, detailed evaluations of mechanical properties like tensile strength, creep resistance, and fatigue behavior under various service conditions are lacking [ 332 ,  333 ]. The absence of a standardized and accessible reference for HEAs’ composition–structure–property relationships has restricted their practical application.

sections.heading: Future perspectives
paragraphs: HEAs are at the forefront of advanced materials research, offering exceptional compositional flexibility, properties, and functional potential. However, several critical and future implementation challenges must be addressed to move from laboratory to industrial scale and transform the potential into reality. The prospects for HEA development can be outlined in the following key directions:

Advanced predictive modeling and AI integration Currently, techniques such as CALPHAD and machine learning algorithms are being employed to predict phase stability and guide composition selection with acceptable accuracy. The HEAs design is shifting towards integrated computational tools. Accelerated Discovery through combinatorial approaches (Such as Machine Learning, CALPHAD, and DFT) in tandem with high-throughput experiments and simulations is expected to identify new HEA compositions with unique properties faster and more efficiently.

Exploration of functional properties beyond mechanics The next phase of HEA research will expand into magnetic, electrical, shape-memory, and superconducting functionalities, enabling applications in soft magnetics, electronics, and actuators.

Coatings, surface engineering & additive manufacturing HEA-based coatings and additive manufacturing routes offer significant promises for wear resistance and surface functionality in harsh conditions such as marine, nuclear, and aerospace environments.

Improved processability, cost reduction, and environmental issues While some HEAs require complex synthesis (e.g., RHEAs), ongoing work focuses on optimizing fabrication methods, improving microstructural control, and reducing costs through element substitution and process simplification. Environmental issues can also be addressed by using methods such as recycling and using waste and scrap.

Tailored performance in extreme conditions Future HEAs will be engineered for high-temperature, cryogenic, and radiation-rich environments through better control of phase stability, defect engineering, and property tunability.

Standardization and database expansion HEAs instantly needs reliable structural-property databases, standardized testing protocols, and composition-property maps to enable repeatable results and industrial qualifications. A systemized and classified database for HEAs, organized in a manner comparable to the Key to Steel, encompassing chemical compositions, phase structures, preparation paths, and mechanical characteristics, can be a valuable resource for researchers and engineers alike. The database will minimize trial-and-error during alloy design, aid data-driven material choice, and narrow the gap between theoretical design and practical applications. The construction of the database also enables the integrated use of machine learning models and computational design tools, facilitating the rapid discovery of alloys.

Exploration of Non-Equiatomic compositions and minor elements effects Most research has concentrated on equimolar systems, but findings indicate that non-equiatomic compositions can also exhibit exceptional properties and performance [ 65 ]. By adjusting elements, especially through minor elements, it is possible to tune phase stability, improve mechanical properties, and control solid solution formation [ 227 ]. Since not all compositions are suitable for engineering applications, developing accurate design strategies to identify optimal non-equiatomic combinations remains a critical research priority.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: HEAs have opened new horizons in advanced materials, offering high-performance alternatives to many traditional alloys with unique properties and enhanced performance. This article aims to identify the high potential of these materials across a wide range of applications by comprehensively reviewing topics related to them. This review article aims to provide a coherent, multidimensional, and application-oriented framework for the study and development of HEAs. Given the complexity of HEAs, their structural variety, and the wide range of potential applications, an attempt was made to provide a comprehensive and analytical view covering design, fabrication, thermodynamics, economics, and engineering performance. The key findings can be summarized in the following main areas:

Core effects and Phase–Property-performance relationships The four core effects justify peculiar phenomena associated with HEAs and play a decisive role in phase formation, microstructure, and properties of the alloy. The interactions and synergies of these effects are still not fully understood. The tunable crystal structure in these materials has a significant influence on their mechanical properties. High ductility is characteristic of FCC structure alloys, while BCC structures are found to provide higher strength and lower ductility. Balanced strength and ductility can be attained by dual-phase (FCC + BCC) alloys. Proper classification of the phase type and composition structure is crucial for determining the alloy’s final performance. The unique properties of HEAs make them excellent candidates for a wide variety of engineering applications. These applications include wear resistance, corrosion and oxidation protection, industrial tooling, military systems, marine structures, aerospace components, energy technologies, electronic devices, cryogenic environments, catalytic processes, and biomedical applications.

Fabrication and processing routes Various fabrication techniques across solid, liquid, and gas states were investigated, and the fundamental influence of processing routes on the thermodynamics, microstructural evolution, phase stability, and performance of HEAs was highlighted. Selecting the fabrication method that aligns with the desired phase, microstructure, and thermodynamic behavior, which overshadow the performance, is crucial for producing the intended alloy. Combining solid-state processing techniques, such as mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS), enables precise control over the microstructure, allowing for customized performance. Beyond technical aspects, economic considerations, such as recycling strategies, element substitution, and the adoption of cost-effective fabrication methods, were also presented, which are helpful for scalable and cost-effective production.

Thermodynamic–Processing coupling In the thermodynamic design of an HEA, the goal is often to find a composition that minimizes the free energy of the entire system, thereby stabilizing a single-phase solid solution. However, this criterion does not always guarantee solid solution formation. Because minimizing ΔG is a thermodynamic equilibrium criterion, stable phases may not be favored in practical processing (under nonequilibrium conditions) and application situations. On the other hand, a solid solution phase is stable only when ΔH mix  is close to zero and the atomic size difference is slight; otherwise, it spontaneously transforms into an intermetallic phase (or even an amorphous phase). As a result, the lowest ΔG does not guarantee that the final structure will have the expected microstructure or mechanical properties; other factors such as diffusion kinetics (i.e., processing time), processing route, rapid solidification or quenching (overall processing conditions), and application requirements must also be considered.

Outlook and challenges Despite significant progress, several aspects, particularly the interaction between core effects, phase evolution, and thermodynamic stability, still require a deeper understanding. Future progress will depend on integrating thermodynamic modeling, high-throughput computational screening, machine learning, and process simulation to enhance the understanding of complex systems. Focusing on scalable, interdisciplinary aspects, the exploration of non-equatomic compositions, the effects of minor elements, and the development of effective, low-cost solutions will accelerate the transition of HEAs from research labs to industry, enabling the creation of next-generation materials with customizable performance for key applications.

tables.caption: Possible effects of key elements in HEAs on phase formation and material properties
rows: Al additions convert FCC structures to BCC phases and enhance solid-solution strengthening. At high Al content, brittle intermetallic phases form, increasing hardness and wear resistance but reducing ductility
Fe with ferromagnetic properties increases solid solution strengthening and yield strength in HEAs
Ni stabilizes FCC solid solutions and improves ductility and toughness. It also enhances corrosion resistance and lowers stacking-fault energy in CoCrFeMnNi-type HEAs

It promotes the formation of the FCC phase, which tends to segregate within the intergranular regions and may lead to the precipitation of Cu-rich spherical nanophases, thereby enhancing the overall mechanical performance of the high-entropy alloy
It may lead to the formation of intermetallic compounds, which can adversely affect the strength and ductility of the HAEs

Co strongly promotes single-phase FCC solid solutions (with Fe and Ni) in HEAs, and a small amount of its addition yields alloys with excellent ductility, wear resistance, and toughness. In addition, it prevents the alloy from breaking when it cools

Cr with intrinsic ferromagnetic properties forms stable passive oxide films, significantly enhancing corrosion and oxidation resistance. It also stabilizes BCC phases at high content, contributing to high-temperature strength

Due to its large atomic radius, Ti introduces lattice distortion and promotes a higher content of HCP/BCC phases. Moderate Ti raises strength and hardness via solid-solution and ordered precipitation; excess Ti yields brittle intermetallics
V is a refractory element that significantly boosts hardness and wear resistance but reduces ductility. It may promote high-temperature strength
W is a heavy refractory that substantially hardens HEAs by solid-solution strengthening. It gives exceptional high-temperature strength and hardness
Nb raises hardness and wear resistance. It stabilizes BCC (and laves) phases, boosting high-temperature strength and creep resistance
Mo is a refractory element that greatly increases hardness and wear resistance. It enhances high-temperature performance

The addition of Ta in HEAs causes a phase structure change from FCC to BCC or mixed structures, increases the stability of multiple phases, and provides significant improvements in hardness and Young’s modulus, although toughness may be reduced. Ta also increases resistance to high-temperature oxidation by forming stable oxide layers, such as α-Al₂O₃, and prevents surface scaling
It typically segregates into the interdendritic regions, which in turn renders the dendritic FCC domains relatively unstable

The alloy’s plasticity increases with the addition of Sn. At low Sn concentrations (e.g., 0.01), the microstructure typically consists of a single-phase FCC solid solution. As the Sn content rises, both strength and plasticity exhibit notable improvement. At higher concentrations (e.g., around 0.05), the alloy exhibits Maximum elongation. However, further addition of Sn promotes the precipitation of hard and brittle intermetallic phases, leading to reduced ductility
Excessive incorporation may lead to the formation of intermetallic compounds, thereby compromising the alloy’s strength and ductility. Controlled addition can enhance corrosion resistance

Mn significantly improves the strength, thermal stability, and high-temperature hardness (red hardness) of HEAs. It may reduce the alloy’s oxidation resistance while simultaneously contributing to cost reduction
May result in improved strength. One of its most important effects may be its antibacterial properties

Minimal B additions in HEAs such as HfMoNbTaTiZr cause (Hf,Zr)B₂ boride precipitation at grain boundaries, markedly raising grain-boundary hardness and cohesion. This intergranular strengthening improves work hardening and ductility in refractory HEAs This can improve the high-temperature compression performance and wear resistance of HEA

Silicon addition in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), such as FeCoNiAlSix and FeCrNiAl₀.₇Cu₀.₃Six, promotes phase transformation toward stable BCC structures, enhances hardness and thermal stability, and significantly improves corrosion resistance by facilitating the formation of a protective passive film. Si can improve compressive strength
Adding C to Fe-based HEAs forms carbides in HEAs, significantly boosting hardness and yield strength. However, carbon typically lowers toughness and ductility when present in high amounts
